title: Ukraine Drone Campaign Hits Yandex Data Centres as SpaceX Moves to Become a US Mobile Carrier
subhead: Kyiv's third strike on Russia's biggest internet company in a week takes a major AI and consumer platform partly offline, while SpaceX's $8bn spectrum deal reshapes US wireless competition and the 6G standards fight splits along geopolitical lines.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Yandex Data Centres for the Third Time in a Week
sections.body:
Yandex, Russia's largest internet company, was forced to suspend operations at a data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow, after a Ukrainian drone strike damaged the facility, according to the BBC. The company said no one was injured but that some services were unavailable, and that connectivity was being restored.

The strike was the third on Yandex infrastructure in a week: facilities in Sasovo (Thursday) and Kaluga (Friday) were hit earlier, degrading services including its AI chatbot and smart home products. Yandex had said two of its five data centres were affected and that it was 'very difficult to predict' when they would return online. The company, which operates a search engine, taxi, and food-delivery apps used by tens of millions, confirmed the Vladimir damage via Telegram.

Kyiv has said it targets facilities that generate revenue for Moscow's war effort and that the strikes could force Russia to divert resources to repairs. The attacks continued alongside broader strikes on both sides: Ukrainian officials reported at least 20 people killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia on Saturday and six injured in Dnipropetrovsk region overnight. The Yandex strikes came hours after US President Donald Trump publicly urged Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries as part of a diesel-supply arrangement criticised in Europe.
sections.whyItMatters: Data centres have moved from the periphery to a front-line target. Repeated strikes on a single commercial operator degrade a country's consumer internet and AI services at once, and they signal that digital infrastructure is now treated as war-sustaining infrastructure — by both sides, since Russia has also struck Ukrainian data centres and driven some firms to relocate servers abroad.

sections.heading: SpaceX's $8bn Spectrum Bet Puts It on Track to Be a US Mobile Carrier
sections.body:
SpaceX agreed to acquire 100% of Grain Management's 800MHz spectrum portfolio, giving it up to 14MHz of paired lowband spectrum that penetrates walls and rooftops — the missing piece in its hybrid satellite-terrestrial network plan, according to Light Reading. The Wall Street Journal reported the price at $8 billion in cash; the deal requires FCC approval. (Grain had itself bought the portfolio from T-Mobile in August 2026 for $2.9bn plus 600MHz spectrum.)

The move is a direct competitive threat to US carriers. In Friday trading, AT&T fell 6.44%, T-Mobile nearly 10%, and Verizon 5.7%, while tower companies rallied — Crown Castle up 14.76%, American Tower 8.46%, SBA Communications 7.19%. Analysts at Recon Analytics had earlier predicted the 800MHz block would end up with Starlink as 'the foundation of a terrestrial voice layer.' Notably, analysts still say SpaceX needs an MVNO deal, since AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile have so far declined to host Starlink.

Separately, the FCC has already approved SpaceX to deploy 15,000 direct-to-device satellites with a nine-year completion window, and SpaceX is lobbying via the 'Grain' spectrum to be recognised as a major mobile carrier.
sections.whyItMatters: Buying lowband spectrum is how SpaceX converts a satellite service into a full terrestrial carrier that can reach ordinary handsets. If the deal clears the FCC, a single launch company would hold both orbital and licensed ground spectrum — a level of vertical integration no incumbent carrier can match, and the reason carrier stocks dropped on the announcement.

sections.heading: China's CXMT Claims Breakthrough on Higher-Density DRAM Cell Design
sections.body:
China's memory chip champion ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) reported 'key progress' on a new memory cell structure pursued by Samsung and SK Hynix, according to SCMP. President Cao Kanyu said at an industry event in Shanghai that CXMT plans to roll out a server-memory product based on the design by the end of 2026.

The design is a '4F square' cell, where each memory cell occupies an area of four square F (F being the minimum semiconductor line width), versus the mainstream 6F square used in commercial DRAM today. Fitting more cells onto a chip raises storage density — the core battleground in DRAM as AI servers demand ever more memory bandwidth.

The claim matters against the backdrop of an AI-driven memory boom: the BBC reports Samsung expects operating profit of 107.4 trillion won (~$80bn) for the quarter to end-September, its fourth consecutive record, driven by memory demand for AI data centres, with full results due end of October.
sections.whyItMatters: Density is the metric that decides DRAM leadership, and 4F² is where the incumbents are heading next. A credible CXMT path to it — even if the timeline slips — narrows the technology gap that export controls were designed to preserve, and lands as memory makers post record profits from AI demand.

sections.heading: 6G Standards Fight Splits Into 'Evolution' vs 'Revolution' Camps
sections.body:
A contest over the shape of the 6G core network has broken out inside the 3GPP standardisation body, according to Light Reading, mirroring the wider US-China technology contest and threatening to produce two competing 6G systems.

Ericsson and Nokia, backed by European and US operators, favour an evolutionary approach — a lightly modified 5G core with AI kept in a separate domain. Huawei is pushing a more radical redesign. Ahead of a recent 3GPP plenary in Madrid, 17 non-Chinese operators, including all European and US incumbents, signed a joint position paper calling for 'evolution as the starting point' in 6G architecture, with the 5G core as 'an important architectural foundation for 6G.' Vodafone R&D head Luke Ibbetson said flatly: 'The 6G core is a very lightly tweaked version of the 5G core. It's not a new thing.'

Delegates from Huawei and its European rivals still attend the same sessions; the 3GPP has survived the first rounds of 6G standardisation, per the report, but the architectural split persists.
sections.whyItMatters: The core is the brain of a mobile network — it decides routing, policy, and increasingly where AI functions sit. If the split hardens, operators face a choice between two incompatible architectures, which is exactly the fragmentation that network-geopolitics analysts have warned about since 5G.

sections.heading: China-Linked Hackers Pose as US Officials to Target AI Policy Experts
sections.body:
A group tracked as TA419, described by cybersecurity firm Proofpoint as China-aligned, impersonated a former senior White House technology official, a former State Department economist, and a senior Anthropic employee to break into the cloud accounts of AI policy experts, according to Defense One. Targets were researchers at think tanks, universities, and law firms.

The lures were invitations to join a fictitious 'AI Policy Advisory Committee' or contribute to a purported Senate Foreign Relations Committee report on AI export controls and supply chains. The impersonated figures included Lynne Parker, former principal deputy director of the White House OSTP, and Heidi Crebo-Rediker, the State Department's first chief economist. Victims who engaged were sent links to a fake OneDrive page to steal Microsoft credentials. Proofpoint did not say how many were targeted or whether any accounts were compromised; it noted a similar February attempt impersonating an Anthropic employee with the subject 'Request for Feedback on Military Integration of Claude.'

Separately, the Register reports the FBI seized seven domains linked to tools from Chinese firm Integrity Technology Group, used by Beijing-backed operatives to scan a South Carolina power company and other critical infrastructure. Seven governments — US, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and Spain — issued a joint advisory; CISA added five CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
sections.whyItMatters: The target set is the point: the attackers went after the people who write AI export-control and supply-chain policy, not just the systems they run. Combined with the infrastructure seizures, it shows espionage campaigns now run in parallel with tooling disruption aimed at state-linked cyber firms.

sections.heading: China Launches Guowang and Yaogan Satellites as Megaconstellations Multiply
sections.body:
China completed its ninth and tenth launches of September, sending Guowang — its national broadband megaconstellation — and Yaogan-40 satellites into orbit aboard a Long March 8A, SpaceNews reports from Helsinki, setting up an intense Q4 manifest.

The launches land as orbital real estate fills up. SpaceNews notes Amazon wants more than 5,000 satellites, Blue Origin has proposed another 5,400, and Chinese companies have filed plans 'encompassing vastly more,' under a headline of intensifying resource competition. The FCC's approval of SpaceX's 15,000 direct-to-device satellites is part of the same wave.

In adjacent orbital-telecom news, LMT Group and Novaspace announced a partnership to develop a 5G/6G satellite communications hub strategy in Latvia, and open-source RAN project OCUDU released version 26.10 adding satellite connectivity and new 5G capabilities.
sections.whyItMatters: Megaconstellation filings are effectively claims on orbital slots and spectrum. With Guowang expanding, Amazon and Blue Origin queuing, and SpaceX approved for 15,000 more, the practical constraint shifts from launch capacity to regulatory and spectrum clearance — the slowest gate in the system.

bottomLine: The day's clearest signal is that infrastructure once considered civilian is being contested as strategic. Ukraine's third drone strike in a week on Yandex data centres knocked parts of Russia's largest internet and AI platform offline, demonstrating that a data centre can be a war target with immediate consumer impact. On the commercial side, SpaceX's $8bn purchase of lowband spectrum — with carriers' shares falling on the news — moves a launch company toward being a full US mobile carrier, while the 6G core fight inside the 3GPP shows the US-China split is now shaping standards, not just hardware. In chips, CXMT's 4F² DRAM claim and Samsung's record $80bn quarterly profit capture the two sides of the AI memory boom: incumbents cashing in, and China inching closer to closing the density gap. And in cyber, TA419's impersonation of US officials to reach AI-policy experts shows espionage is now aimed at the people who write the export-control rules.
sources: BBC News, SCMP, Defense One, The Register, SpaceNews, Light Reading, Proofpoint (via Defense One), Recon Analytics, Wall Street Journal, CISA, FBI
